title: Taming Stochastic Gradient Descent: Almost Sure Convergence and Saddle-Point Avoidance under $(L_{0},L_{1})$-Smoothness
claim: Our tamed method reaches the target accuracy far more reliably than vanilla and clipped baselines across iteration budgets.
layout: single line plot, success rate vs iterations, error bars and shaded bands
description: A single line chart titled "Phase retrieval". The x-axis is iterations T from 2000 to 8000. The y-axis is success rate for reaching gradient norm below epsilon, from 0% to 100%. Five series carry markers, error bars and translucent shaded bands. Three tamed SGD variants are solid lines: red with norm cubed (highest, about 92% at 8000), purple with exp of norm (about 85%), and green with norm to the fifth (about 80%). Clipped SGD is an orange dash-dot line that tracks near the green one. Vanilla SGD is a blue dashed line that stays below about 5%. All curves start near 0% at 2000 and 3000 iterations. A legend sits in the upper left. The eye goes first to the red curve and to the gap between it and the flat blue line.
caption: Success rate for achieving an accuracy of 0.001 (in terms of gradient) across different max number of iterations, over 80 runs. Here we compare three instances of (TSGD) with 𝑟(𝑥) = ∥𝑥∥3 (red), 𝑟(𝑥) = ∥𝑥∥5 (green) and 𝑟(𝑥) = exp(∥𝑥∥) (purple), with vanilla (SGD) (blue) and clipped stochastic (CGD) (orange).
abstract: Many optimization problems in machine learning and data science—from deep neural networks to Bayesian inference and beyond—fall outside the standard Lipschitz smoothness framework that underpins the convergence theory of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Motivated by this theory-practice disconnect, we examine the almost sure convergence of the trajectories of SGD in non-convex landscapes under a generalized $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness condition which allows for gradients with superlinear growth (even exponential). We begin by proposing a taming scheme for SGD that achieves almost sure convergence under a generalized ABC-type condition on the gradient noise. Subsequently, to relax this requirement, we introduce a more flexible, dissipative taming scheme which converges almost surely under less restrictive moment bound conditions for the stochastic gradients entering the process. For both taming schemes, we show that the generated trajectories avoid strict saddle points (and/or manifolds thereof) with probability 1 so, generically, both methods only converge to local minimizers.
